newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Senate bans partial-birth abortion.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Senate bans partial-birth abortion.

text.p: The New York State Senate Monday passed a ban on so-called partial-birth abortions, one of a number of state-level efforts to restrict the controversial procedure.
New York's legislation, which passed by a vote of 40-19, would make it illegal for anyone to perform the procedure unless the mother's life is threatened, lawmakers said.
"This is not a pro-life or pro-choice issue," said Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno. "It is simply a question of basic human decency."
Pro-abortion rights forces opposed the bill because it places limits on abortion which do not exist in New York state.

The future of the bill is unclear. State Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver has said the Assembly will not consider the ban unless the procedure is allowed to be used to protect the life -- and health -- of the mother.
The state Senate passed a similar bill last year, but it never went before a vote in the state Assembly.

On a national level, a new measure to ban the controversial medical procedure was introduced last week in the House of Representatives. Other state legislatures are attempting to prohibit the abortion method as well.

The issue has sparked heated debate since a ban was first introduced in Congress in 1995, in part because of the nature of the procedure which involves the partial extraction of the foetus, feet-first, from the birth canal and the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

Recently Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, stoked the controversy when he said he had "lied through my teeth" about the number of such abortions performed each year.
In a published article, he said most of the abortions -- referred to medically as intact dilation and evacuation -- were performed on healthy women with healthy foetuses.
President Bill Clinton vetoed a proposed ban on the procedure last year, arguing it was performed on only a few hundred women whose health was endangered or whose foetuses had terrible deformities.

Clinton said he would sign the bill if it included an exception for cases where the woman's health was at risk. The current bill, like the previous one, provides only for cases where the woman's life, but not her health, is in jeopardy.
The exact number of such abortions performed each year remains unclear. Estimates range from the hundreds to several thousand.

"It is quite frankly akin, or very close, to homicide, and not something that should be practiced in a civilised society," said the bill's sponsor in New York, state Sen. Serphin Maltese, a Republican from New York City. "We must take a stand to condemn this barbaric procedure so that no reputable physician will ever perform it in the future."
